meta.rule: no numbers, no entry - measured entries carry claim+source; others are case-studies or tools

projects.name: ripgrep
projects.blazing: repeatedly benchmarks 10×+ faster than GNU grep on large trees (see the project's own fgrep/grep comparisons in the [GUIDE](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/blob/master/GUIDE.md#benchmarks)).

projects.name: memchr
projects.blazing: SIMD-accelerated; the backbone under `regex` and `ripgrep`.

projects.name: regex
projects.blazing: literal optimizations + SIMD-powered DFA; its docs document multi-x speedups vs naive engines.

projects.name: tokio
projects.description: the async runtime most of this list runs on
projects.blazing: work-stealing scheduler; powers production at AWS, Microsoft, Discord.

projects.name: hyperfine
projects.blazing: statistical warm-up/outlier analysis in a CLI; the tool we benchmark this list with.

projects.name: sux
projects.description: succinct structures: Elias-Fano, rank/select, static functions, minimal perfect hashing
projects.blazing: scales to trillions of keys with very fast queries executed directly on the compressed representation.

projects.name: roaring-rs
projects.description: Roaring compressed bitmaps for IDs, postings and set operations
projects.blazing: own run, v2 methodology (2026-10, quiet 2-vCPU, median of 7): dense union materialize 2.5 ms vs 1879 ms for HashSet (755x) and intersect 12.6 ms vs 1176 ms (93x); at sparse 0.02-0.2% density materialize wins only 4-16x, contains is 6-11x slower than HashSet, and BTreeSet wins count-only scans - density and op semantics decide ([full run](https://github.com/rager306/awesome-blazing-rust/blob/main/runs/roaring-2026-10/RESULTS.md), scope: component).

projects.name: hashbrown
projects.description: SwissTable hash map; the implementation inside Rust's std since 1.36
projects.blazing: open addressing with SIMD control-byte probing.

projects.name: indexmap
projects.description: insertion-ordered hash map + set, O(1) amortized with order
projects.blazing: std-level speed with deterministic iteration.

projects.name: im
projects.description: immutable/persistent collections with structural sharing (archived 2026 - historical entry)
projects.blazing: O(1) clones - cheap snapshots for concurrent and functional workloads.

projects.name: smallvec
projects.blazing: eliminates heap allocation for the common short case.

projects.name: itertools
projects.blazing: zero-cost abstractions, fused adapters.

projects.name: blake3
projects.blazing: ~GB/s on modern x86 (AVX2/AVX-512, per the [project's benchmark table](https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3#benchmarks)); orders above SHA-2/SHA-3.

projects.name: xxhash-rust
projects.blazing: non-crypto hashing at memory-bandwidth speeds.

projects.name: ahash
projects.blazing: documented multi-fold wins over SipHash on hash-map workloads.

projects.name: crc32fast
projects.blazing: 15× faster than naive, via slicing-by-8 and SIMD switching ([crate docs](https://github.com/srijs/rust-crc32fast#performance)).

projects.name: pathfinding
projects.description: BFS, Dijkstra, A*, K-means, CSPs and friends
projects.blazing: the Swiss-army graph-algorithms crate.

projects.name: rstar
projects.blazing: bulk-loaded queries at interactive rates.

projects.name: num-bigint
projects.blazing: Karatsuba multiplication in the num-rational stack.

projects.name: rayon
projects.blazing: near-linear scaling on parallel sort/map in typical workloads.

projects.name: lz4_flex
projects.blazing: no C dependency; the safe configuration avoids `unsafe` and is benchmarked separately from the unsafe-feature build.

projects.name: zstd-safe
projects.blazing: the ratio/speed king of general compression, one call away.

projects.name: bbtree
projects.description: concurrent ordered map built from a cost model
projects.blazing: 5× vs std `BTreeMap` at 1 thread; 12× vs crossbeam-skiplist at 96 threads; map-only swap into fjall/SlateDB/Tonbo/Turso/Lance: 1.16-6.83× end-to-end; p99 5× lower ([design post and benchmark tables](https://github.com/XiangpengHao/bbtree#benchmarks)).

projects.name: crossbeam
projects.blazing: the substrate half of modern lock-free Rust runs on.

projects.name: dashmap
projects.blazing: sharded locking beats global `RwLock<HashMap>` by design.

projects.name: papaya
projects.description: concurrent hash map, read-optimized counterpoint to sharded designs
projects.blazing: built around read throughput with incremental resizing.

projects.name: glommio
projects.blazing: no cross-thread scheduling, direct io_uring.

projects.name: monoio
projects.blazing: io_uring-first, production at scale.

projects.name: io-uring
projects.blazing: one syscall for many ops - the kernel interface built to be ignored by no one.

projects.name: redb
projects.blazing: LMDB-class numbers documented in its bench suite; the File backend stays within a ~2× margin against the removed (unsound-in-practice) mmap backend per the 0.14.0 [changelog](https://github.com/cberner/redb/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md); benchmark harness in [`crates/redb-bench`](https://github.com/cberner/redb/tree/master/crates/redb-bench).

projects.name: fjall
projects.blazing: benchmarked against rocksdb/sled with open methodology; bbtree swap-in partner.

projects.name: SlateDB
projects.blazing: cloud-native LSM; bbtree e2e partner.

projects.name: sled
projects.blazing: the project that set the tone for "blazing" claims - treat numbers as historical.

projects.name: qdrant
projects.description: vector database in Rust: filtered ANN search, quantization
projects.blazing: publishes an open benchmark suite that compares engines at comparable recall@k - speed claims are quality-adjusted, not raw.

projects.name: petgraph
projects.blazing: the default choice; algorithmic core used across the ecosystem.

projects.name: rustworkx
projects.description: IBM's graph library (Python API requires adaptation, not drop-in NetworkX; `rustworkx-core` is the pure-Rust crate)
projects.blazing: documented multi-x wins over pure-Python NetworkX at Qiskit scale.

projects.name: oxigraph
projects.blazing: embedded+server SPARQL with active perf discipline; persistence is RocksDB-backed by default (feature-gated in-memory alternative).

projects.name: cozo
projects.blazing: recursive queries as a first-class, stored-procedure-free primitive.

projects.name: fst
projects.description: finite state transducers for large sets and maps with streaming construction
projects.blazing: ~16,000,000 Wikipedia article titles (384 MB of strings) compress to a 157 MB fst with fast prefix/fuzzy queries (author's 2015 measurement - historical, tied to that setup).

projects.name: tantivy
projects.blazing: benchmarked against Lucene, frequently ahead on ingest.

projects.name: aho-corasick
projects.blazing: the prefilter behind regex/ripgrep multi-literal search.

projects.name: winnow
projects.blazing: zero-copy parsing as the default path.

projects.name: sonic-rs
projects.description: SIMD JSON parsing straight into serde-compatible structs (no intermediate tape re-parse)
projects.blazing: published benchmarks vs serde_json and simd-json; the `sanitize` feature needed for LLVM sanitizers costs ~30% in serialization - production builds keep it off ([benchmarks](https://github.com/cloudwego/sonic-rs#performance)).

projects.name: simd-json
projects.description: SIMD JSON parsing into a tape, following the simdjson design in Rust
projects.blazing: performance tracks the C++ simdjson implementation; best numbers require a custom allocator (mimalloc/jemalloc).

projects.name: polars
projects.blazing: documented multi-x wins over pandas on groupby/join; query-optimized, lazy, parallel.

projects.name: apache-arrow-rs
projects.blazing: zero-copy interchange - the "no-serialization" tax advantage.

projects.name: datafusion
projects.description: extensible, Arrow-native SQL query engine for single-node analytics - the engine many Rust data systems embed
projects.blazing: DataFusion 43.0.0 posted the fastest single-node Parquet numbers on ClickBench "hot" runs (2024-11-16, partitioned 14 GB Parquet, c6a.4xlarge 16 CPU / 32 GB) - ahead of DuckDB, chDB and ClickHouse on identical hardware, the first Rust engine to hold first place; over 30% faster than DataFusion 34 (Dec 2023) on the same suite, while the authors concede DuckDB stays slightly ahead on "cold" runs ([post](https://datafusion.apache.org/blog/2024/11/18/datafusion-fastest-single-node-parquet-clickbench/), scope: component; [bench scripts](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench/tree/main/datafusion), [raw data](https://github.com/apache/datafusion/issues/13099)).

projects.name: moka
projects.description: concurrent cache, Rust port of Caffeine ideas: admission/eviction policies, sync and async APIs
projects.blazing: the leverage is Window-TinyLFU admission keeping hot keys resident; hit-ratio studies are published in the wiki.

projects.name: foyer
projects.description: hybrid RAM + disk cache for data-intensive systems
projects.blazing: eviction-policy benchmark harness (hit-ratio benches) lives in the repo - policy choice is measured, not vibes.

projects.name: differential-dataflow
projects.description: incremental data-parallel computation on timely dataflow
projects.blazing: in the author's graph example (10M nodes, 50M edges), a 15 s initial computation answers input changes in ~230 us - about 100,000x faster than recomputing; batched updates average ~5 us each; two workers cut the build from 15 s to ~8 s ([experiments](https://github.com/TimelyDataflow/differential-dataflow/tree/master/experiments)).

projects.name: quinn
projects.blazing: 0-RTT, multiplexed streams without head-of-line blocking.

projects.name: hyper
projects.blazing: the substrate of axum/reqwest; TechEmpower regular.

projects.name: pingora
projects.blazing: in Cloudflare's migration report, ~70% less CPU and ~67% less memory than the previous proxy at the same traffic ([migration report](https://blog.cloudflare.com/how-we-built-pingora-the-proxy-that-connects-cloudflare-to-the-internet/)).

projects.name: axum
projects.blazing: TechEmpower top-tier via hyper.

projects.name: wasmtime
projects.blazing: Cranelift JIT + Spectre-mitigating design; runs in Firefox, Fastly, Docker.

projects.name: rkyv
projects.blazing: zero-copy *access* to the archived representation; validation and full reconstruction are separate, individually costed steps.

projects.name: faer
projects.description: linear algebra foundation: dense matrices, decompositions, eigenproblems
projects.blazing: published benchmark plots against BLAS/LAPACK backends; kernels use runtime SIMD dispatch via pulp.

projects.name: ndarray
projects.blazing: the substrate scientific Rust computes on.

projects.name: nalgebra
projects.blazing: compile-time dims → unrolled SIMD-friendly kernels.

projects.name: candle
projects.blazing: minimal-deps CPU inference that made HF blogs measurable.

projects.name: burn
projects.blazing: backend-agnostic; documented wins from kernel fusion on some models.

projects.name: rapier
projects.blazing: real-time rigid-body simulation benchmarks published with each release.

projects.name: rust-bio
projects.blazing: pairwise alignment, BWT, variant calling - the algorithms section of computational biology.

projects.name: paramo1d
projects.description: mobile blockchain verification client with recursive proofs
projects.blazing: mainnet sync in 48.43 s on a $100 Redmi 15C against its own cold start (4 GB RAM; prepared matrix caches in place); state proof from genesis 10.78 s; 192.2 MiB peak for the verification client process; 249,885-header chain in 7.44 s ([README numbers](https://github.com/ignotusnemo/paramo1d#readme)).

projects.name: arkworks
projects.blazing: the research-grade finite-field/curve stack most new proof systems benchmark against.

projects.name: verus
projects.blazing: SMT-backed proofs checked per PR - bbtree ships proofs in-repo as a performance guard.

projects.name: miri
projects.blazing: runs bbtree and friends' test suites to keep the unsafe honest.

projects.name: shuttle
projects.blazing: thousands of schedules per PR; pairs with fork-based DST (ffs) that caught what Shuttle missed (bbtree issue #9).

projects.name: uringscope
projects.description: eBPF tracer for io_uring (C+BPF companion for Rust io_uring apps)
projects.blazing: named findings with fixes - "BATCH: you pay a syscall per request" and "PUNT: this is where your p99 lives".

projects.name: cargo-flamegraph
projects.blazing: the first tool you reach for when "blazing" needs evidence.

projects.name: criterion
projects.blazing: regression detection with outlier resistance.

projects.name: divan
projects.blazing: allocation & wall-time profiling with less boilerplate.

projects.name: uringscope SKILL.md
projects.description: for the eBPF io_uring tracer: when-to-reach-for triggers phrased as symptoms (p99 regressions, iou-wrk-* thread storms, syscall-per-op drift)
projects.blazing: turns profiling output into named verdicts.

projects.name: zed
projects.blazing: reported ~128-222 MB RSS vs multi-GB VS Code in published comparisons ([zed.dev/compare/vscode](https://zed.dev/compare/vscode)).

projects.name: gpui-kit
projects.description: component library for GPUI ("shadcn for GPUI")
projects.blazing: brings widget completeness to raw GPUI (which critics note lacks text input).

projects.name: crux
projects.description: shared Rust core, native shells (Elm architecture)
projects.blazing: one core, UIs in SwiftUI/Kotlin/React - typegen proves every effect is handled.

projects.name: egui
projects.blazing: the pragmatic winner of the 2026 Rust GUI survey.

projects.name: slint
projects.blazing: embedded-friendly; the other 2026 survey winner.

projects.name: pulp
projects.description: write SIMD kernels once, dispatch to AVX2/AVX-512/NEON at run time
projects.blazing: removes the compile-time SIMD fork dilemma; the scalar path remains the baseline for measurement.

projects.name: cargo-pgo
projects.description: PGO and BOLT for Rust binaries from cargo
projects.blazing: profile-guided inlining and code layout on real workloads; validate on a workload different from the profiling one.

projects.name: gungraun
projects.blazing: deterministic instruction and cache-metric counts for CI regression gates (specific metrics, not a blanket "no noise" claim).

projects.name: dhat
projects.blazing: the tool behind most "we cut allocations 10×" posts.

projects.name: blaze
projects.description: incremental rebuilds beside cargo: keeps the project compiled in memory, recompiles only changed functions (Cranelift) and patches the program cargo built
projects.blazing: author benchmarks, edit-rebuild on real projects, Linux x86-64: ripgrep 508 -> 56 ms, helix 2.15 s -> 116 ms, bun (1.25M lines) 9.11 s -> 451 ms vs cargo build; ~20 ms save-to-run with live edits ([method and per-platform numbers](https://github.com/indexable-inc/blaze/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md)).

projects.name: dbdelve
projects.description: native multi-engine database client on GPUI (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, DuckDB, MongoDB, Redis and more), no Electron/JVM
projects.blazing: author benchmark vs DBeaver 25.3.1 (M1 Pro, 2026-10, median of 5, alternating runs): launch 1.1 s vs 5.2 s, idle memory 133 MB vs 606 MB, 1M-row grid 56 s vs 208 s at 4.9 GB vs 17 GB ([method](https://github.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md)).

projects.name: strict-future-contract
projects.description: RFC draft (by the blake3 author): a pending future that requests a wakeup must be
projects.blazing: mechanism claim, no benchmark: snoozing hidden in common patterns (select! by reference through the `Pin<&mut _>` impl, `StreamExt::next`) withholds wakeups and surfaces as futurelock deadlocks, missed wakeups, timeouts and UI stutter ([Futurelock case study](https://rfd.shared.oxide.computer/rfd/0609)).

projects.name: nachalnik
projects.description: transparent agent runtime (context, tools, permissions and requests as explicit user-editable state, append-only event log, no `unsafe`, no sockets in the core) plus `kamchatka`, a terminal agent with a kernel-sandboxed shell (Landlock + seccomp, asked when a command *actually tries* the network), per-item context control with undo, and byte-for-byte reproducible releases
projects.blazing: mechanism claims, no benchmark: every documented invariant has a red test, `cargo mutants` survivors get a test or a written excuse it can't be caught, model-introspection eval makes "why do you think that?" falsifiable, and build-profile decisions in Cargo.toml carry their own measurements (fat LTO 10.8 MB vs 14.3 default; `opt-level="s"` saves 3.5 MB for 15-18% slower screen draws).

projects.name: taffy
projects.description: flexbox and CSS Grid layout engine in Rust powering Servo, Bevy, Zed (GPUI), Slint and Lapce; per-node fixed-size measure cache with bit-packed keys (two `Option<f32>` + available space in one `u64`, requested-axis bits hidden in f32 sign bits), spec-conformance tests generated from CSS Working Group fixtures by the `gentest` tooling
projects.blazing: author benchmarks vs Yoga 0.4.0 (M1 Pro, criterion, commits pinned): deep 100k-node hierarchies 63.8 vs 76.8 ms and super-deep 472 µs vs 555 µs (-58..-71% vs its own 0.2 after cache rework), but wide 100k-node trees 247 vs 136 ms - ~1.8x slower there; regressions published alongside wins in-tree ([method and full tables](https://github.com/DioxusLabs/taffy/blob/main/benches/results-2023-02-08.md)).

projects.name: flashraw
projects.description: memory-safe camera RAW decoder in Rust: ~40 formats, 1,980 of 2,016 raw.pixls.us corpus files decode, multithreaded even single-stream codecs (lossless JPEG, Nikon, Pentax) via speculative parallel decoding, explicit SIMD kernels (SSSE3/SSE4.1, NEON, WASM SIMD128), fused single-pass RAW-to-RGB on CPU or GPU (WGSL for Metal/Vulkan/DX12/WebGPU), bounds-checked parsing with pre-checked allocation limits and 15 in-tree fuzz targets; Rust/C/C++/Python (NumPy zero-copy)/WASM bindings plus a LibRaw-compatible C API subset
projects.blazing: author benchmark vs LibRaw 0.22, RawSpeed, rawler, rawpy, dcraw (62 popular + 159-file corpus, median of 7 runs in a fresh process per (file, library, mode, threads), every build flag documented, raw data and charts in-tree): RAW-to-RGB 8.8x vs LibRaw on Ryzen 9700X and 15.4x on M1 Ultra all-cores (59/59 files), 2.1x/1.8x single-threaded; RawSpeed is faster single-threaded on Apple Silicon (median 0.83x) - a "where FlashRaw is not the fastest" section is part of the docs ([method](https://github.com/ybouane/flashraw/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md)).

projects.name: eg-strider
projects.description: collaborative text editing on the Eg-walker event-graph lineage (plain index-based operations, CRDT-like state built only during concurrent merges); reverse piece table with a finger search (8-byte pieces stay in L1/L2, surviving text copied exactly once, deleted text never copied), cheap-path-first merging (non-overlapping concurrent edits just shift by the net length change; CRDT fallback only inside conflicting spans), run/causality planning maintained incrementally on append, lazy sectioned files (header/text/history, history cut at linear boundaries so reopen reads header+text only), struct-of-arrays layouts (16-byte runs vs 64), zstd on text and history
projects.blazing: author benchmarks vs diamond-types, Yjs, Loro and Automerge (median of 100 runs, libraries cycling through traces so the branch predictor cannot overfit one trace, merge times include appending since wins moved work out of the merge): merge 2.45-10x vs diamond-types and up to 1091x vs Automerge, reopen ~25x vs whole-file load (0.03-0.08 ms), steady-state memory more than halved; honest losses published - Automerge snapshots are smaller on some traces (C1: 116 vs 141 KiB). Research-grade: no input validation, a single invalid event panics; a validating server in front is the proposed fix ([post](https://jzhao.xyz/posts/eg-strider)).

projects.name: gitoxide
projects.description: pure-Rust implementation of Git (gix/ein CLI + a 60-crate library workspace) built around memory-mapped, zero-copy pack and object-database access (Apache-2.0/MIT, very active: 12.1k stars, last push 2026-10-27)
projects.blazing: maintainer-published benchmark discussions with numbers: the pure-Rust Sirocco decompressor (Oct 2026) took commit traversal 187k -> 259k commits/s (1.33x) and pack indexing 1.27x ([discussion](https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/discussions/3084)); the zlib-rs compression path measured 1% faster than zlib-ng ([discussion](https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/discussions/1966)); the closed issue #1 documents gix beating git at pack verification on the Linux kernel pack - 1.41x at 3 threads, 1.72x at 4, widening with core count while git degrades past 3 ([issue](https://github.com/GitoxideLabs/gitoxide/issues/1)) - that comparison is from 2020 and screenshot-based. *Needs: a fresh methodical verify-pack run to retire the 2020 screenshot evidence.*

projects.name: oxc
projects.description: the JavaScript Oxidation Compiler: Oxlint, Oxfmt, parser, transformer and minifier in Rust (MIT, VoidZero-backed, powers Rolldown/Vite's bundler; active daily)
projects.blazing: official benchmarks vs named baselines, each with a dedicated public bench repo: Oxlint 50-100x faster than ESLint depending on CPU cores ([bench-javascript-linter](https://github.com/oxc-project/bench-javascript-linter) - hyperfine mean±σ over 10-20 runs, named hardware, VS Code/Vue Core/Sentry codebases), with the Oxlint 1.0 table at 615.3 ms multi-threaded vs 33.481 s for ESLint (~54x; single-thread 1.840 s, ~18x); parser at least 3x faster than SWC and 5x than Biome (oxc's own caveat: Biome emits a CST, not apple-to-apple; [bench-javascript-parser-written-in-rust](https://github.com/oxc-project/bench-javascript-parser-written-in-rust)); Oxfmt 3x faster than Biome and 35x faster than Prettier ([bench-formatter](https://github.com/oxc-project/bench-formatter)); criterion benches per component in `tasks/benchmark` run on CodSpeed every push with per-PR baselines.

projects.name: ntex
projects.description: framework for composable async network services (HTTP, WebSockets) on selectable tokio/compio/neon runtimes (Apache-2.0/MIT, active, MSRV 1.88)
projects.blazing: third-party rewrk hello-world bench (Ryzen 9 5900X, `rewrk -t 24 -c 500 -d 30s`): 843,766 req/s at 4.5 MB peak memory vs hyper 768,859 req/s at 12.4 MB and axum 768,607 req/s - about 10% under actix-web's 933,297 req/s at a third of its 13.6 MB memory ([results and method](https://github.com/programatik29/rust-web-benchmarks/blob/master/result/hello-world.md)).

projects.name: statico
projects.description: minimal benchmark-grade HTTP server that serves a single configurable static response from memory, built as a runtime testbed: stock tokio, smol and four io_uring runtimes (monoio, compio, tokio-uring, glommio) behind a `--runtime` flag, with per-worker single-threaded runtimes, SO_REUSEPORT load balancing and pre-encoded zero-allocation responses on io_uring
projects.blazing: author benchmark, 1024 connections, minimal static in-memory responses, no logging, CPU pinning where applicable ([README table](https://github.com/awgn/statico#performance)): statico (monoio) 1,436,420 req/s at 4 threads (656,517 at 1) vs nginx (return) 832,082, actix-web 798,809, Go fasthttp 605,603 at 4 threads - 1.7-2.4x ahead; all four io_uring runtimes land 1.14-1.44M req/s at 4 threads vs 1,071,433 for stock tokio; load generator and hardware are not named in the README.

projects.name: plumbrs
projects.description: HTTP/1.1+HTTP/2 load generator and Rust HTTP-client benchmarking harness (hyper, reqwest, tokio-uring, monoio, compio backends) with coordinated-omission-corrected latency per Gil Tene's HdrHistogram method
projects.blazing: self-run in-repo charts: tokio-uring client 382K RPS on one thread scaling to 1.1M at 4 and hyper 198K -> 724K, reported above wrk on HTTP/1.1; hyper-h2 187K -> 689K RPS above rewrk on HTTP/2 ([numbers and charts](https://github.com/awgn/plumbrs#performance)) - no hardware, server, or competitor-version methodology published, so author-claim until replicated.

projects.name: jaq
projects.description: jq clone in Rust (MIT, active, jaq-3.0; core audited by Radically Open Security): drop-in `jq` CLI plus embeddable thread-safe `jaq-core` library, adding YAML/CBOR/TOML/XML
projects.blazing: self-run benchmark with public in-repo methodology ([bench.sh](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/01mf02/jaq/main/bench.sh): user time via `/usr/bin/time -f %U`, min of 3 runs, AMD Ryzen 5 5500U) vs jq 1.8.1 and gojq 0.12.18 ([full table](https://github.com/01mf02/jaq#performance)): group-by on 1M items 260 ms vs 1790 ms for jq (~7x) and 1580 ms for gojq, sort 90 ms vs 430/550, 100k `def`s 50 ms where jq-1.8.1 errors out (N/A), `upto` 8192 in 0 ms (below timer resolution) vs 440 ms; fastest on 20 of 31 benchmarks, with the losses in the same table - jq fastest on 5 (reduce, try-catch, pyramid, ack, range-prop), gojq on 6 (e.g. native `flatten`).

projects.name: ruff
projects.description: Python linter and code formatter written in Rust with drop-in Black parity, replacing flake8, isort, pyupgrade, pydocstyle and autoflake in one tool
projects.blazing: README benchmark chart lints the whole CPython codebase from scratch at a claimed '10-100x faster than existing linters (like Flake8) and formatters (like Black)' (methodology: chart image in [README Performance section](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff#performance) only - no written methodology reachable this session, so the range is vendor-claimed, not replicated).

projects.name: hotpath-rs
projects.description: instrumenting profiler: macros wrap functions, locks, channels and async blocks to report time, allocations, and mutex wait-vs-hold across await - the "why is it slow" complement to sampling profilers
projects.blazing: ~39 ns per measured function call vs an uninstrumented baseline in the same run (1041.4 → 1079.9 ns/op on a ~1 µs spin body), 29-66 ns per lock cycle, 47-88 ns per channel send/recv, ~125 ns per future poll, ~30 ns per stream item; dedicated benchmark examples, 100k iterations, ±10 ns run-to-run noise ([methodology](https://hotpath.rs/profiling_overhead)).

projects.name: foldhash
projects.description: non-cryptographic Rust hash-map hasher built on a folded 64×64→128-bit multiply with per-map random seeds, the successor design to ahash and deliberately not DoS-resistant
projects.blazing: author benchmark ([README](https://github.com/orlp/foldhash#performance), crate 0.2.0, Xeon 8481C with `-C target-cpu=native`, stable Rust 1.80.1, 16 key types × 4 map operations, full tables in a linked gist): geometric mean 6.21 ns/op for foldhash-f (7.56 for foldhash-q) vs aHash 8.74 ns and SipHash-1-3 28.70 ns; aHash wins only on medium-long strings when AES-NI is enabled, and the README does not state which crate version the run used.

projects.name: SurrealKV
projects.description: SurrealDB's Rust LSM storage engine, written in-house to replace the C++ RocksDB library, with a radix-tree memtable, a commit ring that batches a burst of commits into one disk flush, and opt-in time-travel versioning
projects.blazing: vs RocksDB at synchronous durability (each engine flushes before acknowledging), crud-bench on a bare-metal Threadripper 9970X, 500k keys, 48 threads: 7.95× point reads, 6.10× updates, 8.24× deletes, 73.7× point reads vs SlateDB - while reporting 1.88× slower creates than RocksDB without sync ([methodology + one-command repro](https://surrealdb.com/blog/we-are-replacing-rocksdb-with-surrealkv-1-0)).
